extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors (combinatorics/finite geometry/classroom projects)
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing and analyzing Latin squares, mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS), their connection to affine planes, and using these structures to play and study tic-tac-toe-style games; includes classroom project and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Latin square
rubrics_metrics.description: A square in which each symbol (letter or number) appears exactly once in each row and each column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are given (two 4×4 Latin squares). Exercise 1.1 asks students to verify that each letter appears exactly once in each row and column of the example squares. The alphabet may be letters or the natural numbers 0,1,2,... as representatives modulo n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality of two Latin squares (Graeco-Latin square)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Latin squares are orthogonal if, when overlapped, each ordered pair of symbols (one from each square) appears exactly once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Graeco-Latin square example is shown (overlap of two 4×4 squares). Exercise 1.1/1.2 ask students to verify that each ordered pair appears exactly once in the overlapped square; this is the operational test for orthogonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares (MOLS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of Latin squares of the same order such that every pair of squares in the set is orthogonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the example of three 4×4 squares that are pairwise orthogonal (MOLS of order 4). Representations using the numbers 0..n−1 are shown. Exercises ask students to construct additional Latin squares and to determine orthogonality relationships among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete set of MOLS (maximum size ≤ n−1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete set of MOLS of order n is a set of n−1 mutually orthogonal Latin squares; there can be at most n−1 MOLS of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument sketch: arrange first rows in ascending order; entries in a certain column of the second row must be distinct and different from 0, giving only n−1 possibilities. Exercises and discussion ask students to understand this bound and the definition of completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal construction L_k (formulaic construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: define L_k with entries L_k(i,j) = k·i + j (mod n) (i,j,k in alphabet 0..n−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are asked to verify that each L_k is a Latin square and that L_k and L_j are orthogonal when n is prime. Exercises (e.g., 1.6 and 1.11) guide verification and outline a proof that this construction yields the maximum possible number of MOLS when n is prime (produces n−1 MOLS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime vs composite n for the orthogonal construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The orthogonal construction above yields n−1 MOLS precisely when n is prime; the construction fails (does not always produce Latin squares or orthogonality) when n is not prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 1.7 and 1.11 ask students to construct examples for n=4,5,6 and to show why the method works for prime n and fails when n is composite (provide counterexamples or show the construction doesn't produce Latin squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between MOLS and affine planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Given MOLS of order n, one can draw an affine plane of order n by treating points as grid positions and drawing a line for each set of positions sharing a common symbol in a given square; in this geometry any two lines meet once or are parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.8–1.10 instruct students to construct affine planes from MOLS (order 4, 5, 7 examples). The text notes the number of lines (example: 12 lines for order 3 construction) and emphasizes the parallel/meeting properties that characterize an affine plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tic‑tac‑toe on an affine plane: rules and pedagogical usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Game rule: a player wins by marking all positions on a line; the game is played on the affine plane (constructed from MOLS) rather than a standard n×n grid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor notes: students must play the game to understand strategy arguments; play in class or collect game sheets. Tournament suggestion: best-of-three matches, coin toss to decide who goes first. Note: perfect play yields a win for the first player, but students' mistakes make play instructive. Repeated play is encouraged for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing variant games as student projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be encouraged to design new games on affine planes (e.g., last-unclaimed-point-on-a-line loses; or require n−1 marks on a line to win).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such projects may be easy or extremely difficult to analyze strategically; instructors are encouraged to have students explore and attempt analysis. These are proposed as class projects to deepen understanding and creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise/veriﬁcation checklist for student mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete tasks students should perform to demonstrate understanding: verify Latin-square properties, verify orthogonality (each ordered pair appears once), construct addition/multiplication tables modulo n, construct L_k for given n, and draw the corresponding affine plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 1.1–1.11 enumerate these tasks (e.g., verify examples in (1),(2),(3),(4),(5),(7); construct tables modulo 5; build MOLS for n=3,4,5,7; prove the orthogonal construction properties). These exercises serve as assessment tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known existence results and the Fundamental Question
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental question: for which n are there complete sets of MOLS? Known facts: complete sets exist for orders that are prime powers (n = p^k); it is unknown for other n; there is no complete set of order 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The epilogue explains current state of knowledge and notes the computational difficulty (combinatorial explosion) that makes some cases intractable; this forms background for projects and theoretical exploration.
